content: Tropical sprue is a chronic diarrheal disorder of unknown cause that primarily affects individuals in tropical and endemic regions. The first description of a disease resembling tropical sprue was reported in Belgium. The term tropical sprue was introduced by Sir Patrick Manson. Tropical sprue is categorized into two phases based on the duration of symptoms: an acute phase and a chronic phase. The exact pathophysiology of tropical sprue remains unclear. However, it is believed to involve intestinal inflammation following an episode of diarrhea. This inflammation damages the intestinal villi and leads to lymphocytosis in the intestinal wall. A deficiency of the lactase enzyme results in carbohydrate malabsorption, while dysfunctional enterocytes contribute to steatorrhea. The specific cause of tropical sprue is unknown, but various bacterial species have been identified in patients with the condition. Tropical sprue is a diagnosis of exclusion, meaning it must be differentiated from other malabsorption disorders, such as celiac disease. Tropical sprue is now a rare diagnosis, with the highest prevalence observed in tropical countries. Risk factors for developing tropical sprue include a prior episode of infectious diarrhea and travel to endemic areas. Screening for tropical sprue is not recommended, as it is a rare disease and a diagnosis of exclusion. Tropical sprue typically progresses through an acute and a chronic phase. It often follows an episode of infectious diarrhea. Patients usually present with chronic, non-bloody diarrhea and malabsorption. In the chronic phase, symptoms of vitamin B12 and vitamin A deficiencies may develop. With appropriate treatment, the prognosis is excellent. In the acute phase, patients with tropical sprue may experience diarrhea, bloating, flatulence, fever, and myalgias. In the chronic phase, symptoms of malabsorption become prominent. During the acute phase, physical examination findings may reveal signs of dehydration. In the chronic phase, features such as subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord and visual field defects may be observed. There are no specific laboratory findings for tropical sprue, as it is a diagnosis of exclusion. However, blood smears in the chronic phase may show megaloblastic changes. All other potential causes of malabsorption must be ruled out to confirm the diagnosis. There are no electrocardiogram (ECG) findings associated with tropical sprue. X-rays are not useful for diagnosing tropical sprue. CT scans are not directly used to diagnose tropical sprue but can help exclude other conditions, such as inflammatory bowel disease or chronic pancreatitis. MRI is not required for the diagnosis of tropical sprue. Imaging studies are generally not necessary for diagnosing tropical sprue. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy should be performed to obtain a duodenal biopsy. Histological findings suggestive of tropical sprue include intestinal villous blunting and intestinal lymphocytosis. The primary treatment for tropical sprue includes folic acid supplementation and antimicrobial therapy. Supportive care involves ensuring adequate hydration and replacing deficient nutrients, such as iron and vitamin B12. Oral tetracycline is contraindicated in pregnant and lactating women, as well as in children under 8 years of age. The main goals of treatment are to control diarrhea, correct vitamin deficiencies, and cure the disease. Surgery is not required for patients with tropical sprue. Antibiotic therapy alone is the primary treatment modality. Primary prevention measures include drinking clean water and maintaining good hygiene. There are no secondary preventive measures for tropical sprue.
